item.title: She Won a Texas House Seat. Her Rival Says She Can’t Take Office.
item.description:
Few expected a Democrat to win a deep red Texas House seat in and around Fort Worth.

No Republican had lost there in almost two decades. And the Democratic candidate, Ericka Lomick, had suspended her campaign weeks before Election Day amid questions over her eligibility because of a felony conviction.

But then came the Democratic wave that swept across Texas, and Ms. Lomick, whose name remained on the ballot, found herself, despite herself, elected.

The result left Democrats and Republicans scratching their heads — a bizarre footnote in what had been a thorough repudiation of Republicans in Texas. Ms. Lomick sounded stunned herself in a brief telephone interview with The New York Times on the day after the election.

“I’m appreciative of the outcome,” she said. But Ms. Lomick was also uncertain if she could serve.

“I’m waiting for guidance from legal counsel,” she said at the time.

Now the question of whether she can take office is before the Texas Supreme Court.

Lawyers representing her Republican opponent, Alan Blaylock, have filed a petition to the state’s highest court arguing that Texas law prevents her from serving. According to the state election law, someone with a felony conviction cannot be elected to public office, unless the person has been pardoned or “otherwise released from the resulting disabilities.”

Kendall Scudder, the chair of the Texas Democratic Party, said in an interview on Wednesday that Ms. Lomick had met that criteria and believed that she was “absolutely eligible and ready to serve.”

Ms. Lomick, 51, did not respond to a request for comment on the case. A lawyer said to be representing her did not return a call seeking comment.

The ultimate fate of the House seat will not determine control of the chamber. Democrats seized control from Republicans by a comfortable margin on Election Day.

But the legal fight appeared to be a novel one for Texas, at least in recent memory. Questions of eligibility do come up, but usually pertain to whether a candidate lives in the district.

“I’ve never seen one like this,” said Trey Trainor, a longtime election lawyer and former Trump administration official who is representing Mr. Blaylock. Mr. Trainor said the situation was a direct result of Democrats’ surprising strength in Texas this year.

“In a normal year, it wouldn’t have mattered” because the Republican would have won, he added.

Adding to the legal confusion was the fact that Ms. Lomick won not one but two elections: the general election for a two-year term as state representative starting in January, and a special election to serve out the remainder of the current term until the end of this year. Both were held simultaneously on Election Day.

On Monday, Gov. Greg Abbott declined to certify the results of the special election. He would wait for guidance from the court, his spokesman, Andrew Mahaleris, said.

The area where Ms. Lomick ran, known as House District 93, includes parts of Fort Worth and its northern suburbs in Tarrant County. The district was seen as reliably conservative — a Democrat had not won there since 2008 — and was recently represented by Nate Schatzline, a pastor and among the most hard-right members of the Texas House. Mr. Schatzline left office earlier this year to become an adviser to Mr. Abbott on election policy.

Texas Democrats contested every race for statewide office and every State House race in 2026, including those where winning appeared unlikely. Candidates were recruited aggressively and included people who have never run for office before, including Ms. Lomick, said Katherine Fischer, the executive director of the Texas Majority PAC, which worked with the state party to field candidates.

“We found Ericka in the same way that we found a lot of the candidates that we recruited,” via conversations with local groups and other outreach, Ms. Fischer said.

Ms. Lomick expressed interest in running, Ms. Fischer said.

“She’s super personable, and she’s very committed to her community,” she added.

The vetting process included conversations with the candidate, a review of her online and social media presence and a background check done using a private agency.

“It didn’t turn up anything of legal note,” Ms. Fischer said.

What the background check missed was that when Ms. Lomick lived in North Carolina, under a different last name, she was convicted in federal court of mortgage fraud and bank fraud. She served several years in federal prison and was released in 2016.

Ms. Fischer said that all the recruited candidates were asked if they had anything in their past that could be a problem. It was not clear if Ms. Lomick, who later moved to Tarrant County, was asked directly about any criminal convictions.

In filing to run, Ms. Lomick checked a box saying she had never been convicted of a felony, Ms. Fischer said.

The conviction surfaced in September after a political action committee, Protect and Serve Texas PAC, published court documents from the criminal case. Ms. Lomick suspended her campaign later that month.

After that, Mr. Blaylock appeared likely to coast to victory, and turned his attention elsewhere.

“He spent a bunch of time trying to help other people,” said Mr. Trainor, his lawyer.

Mr. Blaylock lost by a narrow margin in the special election and by fewer than a thousand votes in the general.

Mr. Blaylock’s lawyers have asked the Texas Supreme Court to order the secretary of state, who oversees elections, to declare Ms. Lomick ineligible under the law. That would leave the seat vacant, and trigger a special election.

The court gave secretary of state and Ms. Lomick until Monday to file their legal responses.

“She gets to make those decisions of how she chooses to move forward,” said Mr. Scudder, the state Democratic Party chair. Whatever the outcome, he added, the party would fight to keep the seat.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Alaska Republican Narrowly Defeats Independent House Candidate
item.description:
Representative Nick Begich III, a first-term Republican from Alaska, narrowly won re-election against an independent challenger on Wednesday, according to The Associated Press, keeping his seat amid broad losses for the party.

Mr. Begich, the scion of an established liberal political family in Alaska, defeated Bill Hill, a fisherman and former school administrator who ran as an independent, as well as Democratic and Libertarian opponents. Mr. Begich won on the same ballot as former Representative Mary Peltola, the Democrat who won this year’s Alaska Senate race. He had toppled her to win the state’s sole House district by less than three points in 2024.

Mr. Hill’s loss is the latest example of a failed Democratic strategy of betting on independents in Republican states. He was forced to spend time explaining to voters that the Democratic candidate, Eric Hafner, was in federal prison in New York and had never been to Alaska. Even with national Democratic groups spending for Mr. Hill in the last weeks of the race, Mr. Hafner still earned more than 7 percent of the votes in the first round, many of which did not translate to support for Mr. Hill.

Mr. Begich’s win was announced more than two weeks after Election Day, with the incumbent prevailing with 51.4 percent of the vote to Mr. Hill’s 48.6 after the state’s ranked-choice voting tabulation.

While 45 percent of Mr. Hafner’s voters ranked Mr. Hill next, nearly half of them did not rank another candidate, taking their ballots out of consideration in the ranked-choice process, according to a New York Times analysis of unofficial ballot counts from the Alaska Division of Elections.

Mr. Begich campaigned on the investments he had secured for Alaska. He emphasized that seven bills he sponsored had become law, an unusually high number for a freshman member of Congress. And while Mr. Begich had aligned himself with President Trump in the past, he said he would work with both Republicans and Democrats.

Mr. Begich gave a conciliatory message after his victory, saying he looks forward to serving Alaskans “Republican, Independent, Libertarian, and Democrat alike.”

“Alaska’s best days remain in front of us with opportunities for new responsible resource development, new infrastructure, and new industries and the jobs that come with them,” he said in a statement sent to The New York Times.

Mr. Hill, an Alaska Native from the tiny town of Naknek, positioned himself as a champion for working-class affordability while casting Mr. Begich as an out-of-touch multimillionaire. He also sought to pin the effects of rising costs on Mr. Begich, highlighting the incumbent’s support for tariffs and the Iran war.

“I see the price of fuel, the price of food, the loss of health care crushing the spirits of Alaskans,” Mr. Hill said at a campaign event in Fairbanks on Nov. 1.

He added: “We need somebody like us, somebody who understands the pain those decisions are visiting on Alaskan people, somebody who understands what our real hopes and dreams are.”

A businessman from Anchorage, Mr. Begich first ran for the Alaska House seat in 2022, finishing third behind Ms. Peltola and Sarah Palin, the former governor, after the ranked-choice voting process played out. He now holds the seat formerly occupied by his grandfather, who served as a Democrat for one term and was re-elected to a second in 1972 even after he disappeared in a plane crash weeks before the election and was later pronounced dead.

Mr. Begich’s uncle, the former Democratic lawmaker and singer-songwriter Tom Begich, advanced to the runoff for Alaska governor this year, but he withdrew and endorsed the Democrat who placed ahead of him in the primary and ultimately won the office, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.

Mr. Hill said he called to wish Mr. Begich well on Wednesday, adding that “all Alaskans have a stake in his success.”

“This campaign has always been about taking power back from the DC elites and putting it in the hands of the hardworking people of Alaska,” Mr. Hill wrote in a statement released on social media. “While we did not prevail in this election, we will continue that fight together.”

item.title: With Alaska’s Senate Vote Counted, What Comes Next in the Last Frontier?
item.description:
Alaska completed its tally of outstanding votes on Wednesday evening, concluding an extended counting process that captured the country’s attention because of a high-profile Senate race.

A day earlier, The Associated Press declared that Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former congresswoman, had defeated Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent. When Ms. Peltola crossed the necessary threshold, 50 percent plus one vote, that outcome averted the need for the state to move to its ranked-choice tabulation, in which votes for the third- and fourth-place candidates are reapportioned to the leading contenders. With all votes tallied, Ms. Peltola led Mr. Sullivan 50.1 percent to 45.8 percent.

The finished count, scheduled to be certified on Nov. 25, appears to close the book on a political drama, though further legal action from Republicans could still be possible after they accused Ms. Peltola and her allies of cheating. The charge stems from the presence of a second candidate on the ballot named Dan Sullivan, who The New York Times reported last month had been recruited by Ms. Peltola’s allies in an effort to siphon votes from the incumbent.

No specific illegal activity has been alleged, but President Trump has argued that Ms. Peltola should have been disqualified from running. His Justice Department sued unsuccessfully to block the certification of the election if votes for the other Mr. Sullivan were deemed to have prevented the senator from winning. In the end, though, Ms. Peltola won by more votes than the other Mr. Sullivan received.

The Justice Department has also been investigating the recruitment of the other Mr. Sullivan, sending letters to 20 Democrats informing them that they might be targets or asking them to preserve their records, and issuing hundreds of subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Spokesmen for Senator Sullivan and Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who previously stopped short of saying that the election should be certified for Ms. Peltola, did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday.

But Carol Beecher, the state’s director of elections, told reporters on Wednesday that “we plan to certify the election, as per the law.” She said that included the U.S. Senate race.

The count on Wednesday evening also determined control of Alaska’s single U.S. House seat, which will stay in Republican hands after Representative Nick Begich III defeated Bill Hill, an independent supported by Democrats.

Devlin Barrett contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Schools and Bosses Brace for ‘G.T.A. Flu’
item.description:
Vincent Riedel wants to skip school tomorrow. His father, David Riedel, is not so sure, but he’s willing to hear him out.

“We’re currently at the dinner table negotiating,” Mr. Riedel said on Wednesday night as Vincent, 15, a high school freshman in Pittsburgh, made what he found to be a surprisingly convincing argument to spend the next day playing Grand Theft Auto VI instead.

G.T.A. VI, a highly anticipated game over a decade in the making, is rolling out worldwide as the clocks tip into Thursday. The game is expected to leave millions of gamers glued to screens, and parents, teachers, school administrators and H.R. departments managing a flood of sick calls and unexcused absences. It even has a diagnosis, “G.T.A. Flu,” and it’s spreading worldwide.

The game, too, is already a global phenomenon, with wildly positive reviews — and it is engaging deeper sentiments. “It’s a profound moment in capitalism and democracy where people feel like they aren’t getting a fair share,” said Dmitri Williams, a professor of communication at the University of Southern California’s Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism. “It’s not surprising that media with antiheroes would be successful. They’re almost a protest vote.”

But the cultural juggernaut has presented a novel challenge.

Mr. Riedel received a message an English teacher sent to parents on Wednesday morning addressing “rumors” that many students would miss her Thursday classes, which could include “a short assessment on poetry.”

“Hope to see all my wonderful students tomorrow,” she wrote. “They can play all weekend!”

For some companies, the arrival of G.T.A. VI has been months in the making, as employees have booked personal time off well in advance.

A Silicon Valley company, Logitech, offered a new floating holiday for employees to play video games after internal research showed engaging in virtual worlds reduced anxiety and improved productivity, according to a statement. Robin Piispanen, the global general manager and vice president of Logitech, said about 70 percent of his team — which amounts to hundreds — had already planned to cash in the off-day on Thursday.

In Australia, KFC had a tongue-in-cheek excuse to miss work. The chain planned to livestream a faux funeral for a fictional “Ann Alibi” during the Australian workday on Thursday.

The game series has countless fans, and the arrival of the sequel has kindled feelings of nostalgia and camaraderie, experts said. There’s something exciting for a young person who finds community through creating bonds by while gaming, said Carly Kocurek, a professor in game design and experimental media at the Illinois Institute of Technology.

“That sense of belonging is really, really powerful,” she said.

The experience spans generations.

While Logitech is offering paid time off, high schools across the country are bracing for sick days. The scale remains unknown, and different schools have taken different approaches to managing it.

Dr. Jim Brauer, principal of Atlantic High School in Atlantic, Iowa, had a warning for his students and words for the video game’s creators.

“To the students currently developing elaborate excuses,” Dr. Brauer said in a public message on Facebook. “I admire the creativity. I really do. Unfortunately, our attendance procedures remain unchanged.” He went on to address Rockstar Games, the developer of G.T.A. VI.

“You made a game about stealing cars,” Dr. Brauer said. “Tomorrow, you’re apparently planning to steal our entire student body. Thank you?!?”

Esteban Malacara, the academy principal at Jerome I. Case High School in Racine, Wis., thought about addressing the rumors in an email blast but ultimately felt strange writing “‘Grand Theft Auto’ into a correspondence with all the families,” he said on Wednesday night.

“Maybe I don’t want to bring attention to it,” Mr. Malacara said, adding that the game’s release and its implications for attendance at the school of nearly 2,000 students had been “on the radar” since the summer.

He expected at least “some tired kids in seats” on Thursday. Mr. Malacara, 48, has fond memories of skipping high school for record releases at Best Buy.

“I can remember the excitement,” he said. “I can understand it.”

Amar Humphrey, 15, a freshman at Walter H. Dyett High School for the Arts in Chicago, said he had heard chatter that “a lot of people” would not be joining him at school on Thursday. But it was the first that his uncle, Chuck Neely, the school’s student engagement director, was hearing of it.

“Who is going to say ahead of time they’re not coming to school?” Mr. Neely said.

Dillon Fleming, an algebra teacher at Food and Finance High School in New York City, said his students had voted to push back a test from Thursday to Monday. Now he’s left wondering why.

“I would be disappointed in the parents, for the most part, allowing kids to stay home for a video game,” Mr. Fleming said. “That would disappoint me.”

But Mr. Riedel, at least, seemed to be leaning toward letting his son stay home. The teenager had insisted that he already had good grades — and made an even stronger pitch.

“Do you have a favorite game you played as a kid and you love a lot?” Vincent Riedel said. “If they made another one of those, would you want to wake up, play some, and then go to school and wait all day?”

“It’s sort of akin to the Beatles showing up in town,” Mr. Riedel said. “What’s one day of school for an event like that?”

Amelia Nierenberg and Nicole Stock contributed reporting.

item.title: Anthropic Employees Work Hard, but Don’t Expect Them to Play Hard
item.description:
In San Francisco, it is the best of times if you have a big home to sell, a restaurant with a private cellar room or expertise in managing wealth.

For almost everybody else? The cost of living is getting even frothier, and good luck keeping up.

Anthropic, the San Francisco-based company that makes the A.I. chatbot Claude, will begin trading its shares on Thursday for $83 apiece, giving the company a valuation of about $1.5 trillion. Hundreds more San Franciscans will be able to call themselves multimillionaires — and a handful will even become multibillionaires.

But don’t expect to see a flock of super yachts in the San Francisco Bay or a run on Mark Zuckerberg-style gold chain necklaces. In the tech world, Anthropic is known as the oh-so-serious A.I. company, filled with workaholics known as “Ants.”

“They are Ph.D. physicists, and they happen to suddenly find that they have $100 million,” said Mike Simonsen, chief economist at the real estate firm Compass in San Francisco. “It’s definitely not a chasing opulence kind of path.”

And it remains to be seen if their newfound wealth will translate to overflowing riches for the company’s hometown.

A.I. employees, including those from Anthropic, hold secluded meetings several times a week at Terzo, a Mediterranean restaurant near the city’s northern waterfront, said its owner, Ava Nicolai.

They choose the private wine room decorated with bottles from around the world — and then stick to water. They pay the $2,000 food and drink minimum, but do not actually eat or drink enough to reach it, she said.

“They’re never really picky about what they eat,” Ms. Nicolai said. “There aren’t a lot of jackets. Just vests and jeans.”

Anthropic employees have been tight-lipped about the initial public offering, and a company spokeswoman, Danielle Cohen, said she could not say anything because of quiet-period restrictions before the company goes public.

Rick Gordon, a senior managing director at Citizens Private Wealth in San Francisco, says he remembers when Facebook went public in 2012. The young engineers showed up to the company parking lot in Audi R8s, luxury speedsters that cost well into the six figures.

Mr. Gordon, who has guided tech workers through many I.P.O.s, says he’s not seeing anything like that this time around. Anthropic employees talk about homes, furniture and helping family members.

He noted that the attitude was: “We’re busy. We’ve got work.”

Still, the I.P.O. for Anthropic — and a future one expected for OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT — have already had an impact on the San Francisco housing market: Some employees pledged shares to pay for homes months ago.

New data from Compass shows that the median sales price in October for a house in San Francisco surged 29 percent over the past year to $2.39 million. The luxury market had its best month ever, with nine homes selling for more than $10 million and 40 for more than $5 million. (It’s not clear that the purchasers had any connection with Anthropic.)

“San Francisco is really the only hot market left in the country in housing,” Mr. Simonsen said, noting that places like Tahoe, Napa and Hawaii are likely to benefit from the Anthropic I.P.O. because of a run on second homes. “When you have that kind of cash, those are the places to go looking.”

Alexander Lurie, the half brother of Mayor Daniel Lurie, is a luxury real estate agent in the city who works with a number of Anthropic employees.

Many of them had already started buying homes knowing that the I.P.O. was on the horizon, he said, but he expected their access to a huge pile of cash to send prices surging even higher. Many employees will be able to sell 10 percent of their holdings on Day 1.

Unlike wealthy San Franciscans in past generations, Mr. Lurie said, Anthropic employees do not necessarily want to be in Pacific Heights, the neighborhood filled with opulent mansions owned by the entrepreneur Laurene Powell Jobs, Representative Nancy Pelosi and Mimi Haas, a Levi Strauss heir and the mother of the San Francisco mayor.

Anthropic employees are younger, in their 20s, 30s and 40s, and many of them have small children. They are willing to pay well over asking price for spacious homes in family-oriented neighborhoods such as Noe Valley, Cole Valley and Potrero Hill — and they like a modern aesthetic coupled with intense security, usually buying the properties under LLCs, Mr. Lurie said.

“They’re looking to be normal, as normal as possible, on the home front,” he said.

Anthropic has long been shaped by effective altruism, a movement that urges people to give away much of their wealth to the causes that do the most good. All seven of Anthropic’s co-founders have pledged to give away 80 percent of their equity holdings, and the company matches part of the equity that employees pledge to charity.

Some of the new money may flow to causes that seem far removed from San Francisco’s problems. Effective altruism prizes causes it considers neglected and where each dollar goes furthest. Some in Anthropic’s orbit have given to groups like the Shrimp Welfare Project, which gives seafood suppliers machines to stun shrimp before slaughter.

Wild Animal Initiative, which funds animal research, has already received gifts from Anthropic employees, including one of about $100,000 and another of about $50,000, among the largest in its history, said executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb.

The group, whose budget for next year will be about $5.3 million, is in early talks with Anthropic employees about gifts that could reach millions of dollars.

“So much of our strategy has built-in assumptions about a certain level of scarcity,” Mr. Meyer Shorb said. “This is the first tech boom that we really have a chance of directly benefiting from.”

Last week, Anthropic pledged $50 million in grants to local causes by the end of 2027, including to the San Francisco-Marin Food Bank and the San Francisco firefighters’ holiday toy program. Last month, the company announced it would create a public benefit fund starting with 5 percent of its shares.

But Mayor Lurie, who has made private fund-raising an instrumental part of his efforts to improve the city, has said that he has not been able to convince local A.I. leaders to contribute toward city-run efforts.

Some worry that the Anthropic I.P.O. will only exacerbate the wide income chasm in San Francisco, as an increasing number of longtime residents find it more difficult to survive in the city. Some tenants are being offered large sums of money to leave their rent-controlled apartments as property owners seek to charge higher amounts. And Mayor Lurie recently declared a rent emergency after apartment prices rose 26 percent in one year.

Sam Cobbs, the chief executive of Tipping Point Community, an anti-poverty philanthropic organization based in the city, said that Anthropic did provide its technology for six months to nonprofits supported by his organization. But after that, Mr. Cobbs said, Anthropic charged for the continued use of its technology.

“I am anticipating more things to come from Anthropic,” he said. “I haven’t seen any signals yet that that’s happening, but I do expect to see more.”

The flood of A.I. wealth could lead to a changing of the patronage guard in San Francisco, a city where politicians, financiers and business owners have long organized galas and contributed heavily toward arts organizations and civic causes.

Stanlee Gatti, the best man at Gov. Gavin Newsom’s first wedding, has long decorated exclusive parties in the city. But he said he had never been tapped by an Anthropic employee to design anything.

This week, he handled the décor for the City Hall tribute to Ms. Pelosi to celebrate her January retirement. A red, white and blue carpet hugged the grand marble staircase between huge vases of white roses. Nobody mentioned the Anthropic I.P.O., Mr. Gatti said, and he was not aware that any employees were there.

“I’m not sure they’ve learned how to spend their money yet,” he said. “They’ve gone to college, they’ve had an erudite education which has given them this opportunity, but that’s it.”

In his dreams, he said, they would spend with “wild abandon” in San Francisco. On philanthropy, of course. And parties.

item.title: Three MAGA Women Who Defined an Era in Congress Are Exiting
item.description:
The tableau was emblematic of a coarse and gaudy era in Congress: Marjorie Taylor Greene and Lauren Boebert, two die-hard MAGA loyalists, jumping out of their chairs at the 2022 State of the Union to heckle President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

Their outburst — provocative, combatant, intolerant and crude — set the tone and style of a distinct period of politics under the Capitol dome in which Republicans were in charge, loyalty to President Trump was all that mattered and decorum was out the window.

That time, like the G.O.P. majority that presided over it, is coming to an end, and the women who were its archetypes — Ms. Greene of Georgia, Ms. Boebert of Colorado and a third who eventually joined their showboat ranks, Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina — are headed out as well.

All three women, never friends but always frenemies, were elected in 2020. And all will be gone in January, bringing to an official end a brief but colorful moment in Congress dominated by a trio of women whose attention-grabbing tactics, hair and makeup, and constant feuding drew comparisons to the cult favorite film “Mean Girls.”

There was Ms. Greene, a former CrossFit gym owner who became interested in politics only because of Mr. Trump. Ms. Boebert was the former owner of a gun-themed restaurant and bar who did not graduate from high school. Ms. Mace, who was the first woman to graduate from the military academy The Citadel, started out as a mainstream conservative but soon veered sharply toward MAGA, joining the other two on a path through Washington that had involved attracting the spotlight more than legislating.

There are many ways to be successful in Congress. Some members emerge as policy experts. Others rise because they are talented communicators. Still others understand how to build coalitions to push an agenda.

These MAGA women excelled at behaving so provocatively that they built a level of national name recognition that is rare for rank-and-file members in the House. But seemingly with no plan for what to do with the attention, except to generate more of the same, their antics ultimately wore thin, on colleagues and constituents alike.

“They taught as that shitposting for power has its limits,” said Annelise Russell, an associate professor of public policy at the University of Kentucky. “They flew a little too close to the sun, and no one knew how to come back down successfully. These women showed us that you have to at least feign effectiveness.”

She added: “If you don’t deliver anything — for constituents or party leadership — regardless of who you are, you don’t have staying power.”

They, in turn, appeared to grow bored and restless in Congress.

Ms. Greene, who had been among Mr. Trump’s closest allies in the House, abruptly quit Congress last January, announcing her exit days after the president branded her a “traitor” for breaking with him and helping compel the Justice Department to release its files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender.

Ms. Mace did not run for re-election, placing fifth in South Carolina’s Republican gubernatorial primary. Ms. Boebert, the only one of the group who sought to hang on in Congress, was caught up in the blue wave, defeated even after she switched districts to what had been expected to be a safe red seat.

But she said there was a part of her that was ready to move on.

“It’s almost liberating in a sense,” Ms. Boebert told TMZ just before her race was called. “I want to offer condolences to some of my friends who did win.”

Ms. Greene — who last year experienced a kind of political awakening in which she repudiated Mr. Trump and apologized for many of her statements and antics — was once the biggest heat-seeking missile of all.

“I think your fake eyelashes are messing up what you’re reading,” she said to Representative Jasmine Crockett, Democrat of Texas, during a late-night hearing of the Oversight Committee.

Speaking on the House floor as she filed a censure against a Muslim Democratic colleague, she referred to “Representative Ilhan Omar of Somalia — I mean Minnesota.”

Her legislative accomplishments included introducing the bill to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America,” as Mr. Trump insisted. Her fury was not reserved for attacks on Democrats; at one point, she tried unsuccessfully to oust Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker who she said had betrayed the MAGA movement.

Ms. Mace once paraded through the Capitol wearing a tight white tank top with a scarlet “A” emblazoned over her chest. Why? Well, that was beside the point of the stunt .

Ms. Boebert also needed no help in generating headlines, although hers were more often caused by her behavior backfiring on her. She was caught on a security camera vaping and groping her date before being ejected from a performance of the musical “Beetlejuice” in Denver.

During a closed-door session of the House Oversight Committee, as lawmakers were deposing Hillary Clinton in the Epstein investigation, Ms. Boebert leaked a photograph from inside the room to a right-wing blogger, causing Ms. Clinton and her attorneys to storm out and the entire deposition to briefly devolve into chaos.

(Ms. Clinton reacted online to the news of Ms. Boebert’s defeat with two words: “Bye, Felicia.”)

All three women demonstrated a rare streak of independence when it came to their demand for the release of the Epstein files, which for them appeared to transcend their unwavering loyalty to Mr. Trump. The trio withstood immense pressure from a vengeful White House that lobbied them relentlessly to fall in line and join Republican leaders in blocking a vote on the release of the material.

The dynamics of Congress next year, when House Democrats will preside over the largest majority in decades, would have made their brand of theatrics easy to ignore.

Still, the three women have promised to remain part of the public discourse in some yet-to-be-determined form.

“Our founders expected representatives to serve and go back home,” Ms. Boebert said in a video she posted online after her race was called last week. “So, I’m home, I am happy, I have peace and this is not the last you’ll be hearing from me.”

Ms. Greene has emerged as a vocal Trump opponent and part of a growing band of America First loyalists who have split from the president and may coalesce into a political movement. For now, she has attempted to use her star power to launch her own YouTube channel, “Life with MTG.”

Ms. Mace said recently she wanted to recede from the spotlight. “I kind of want to whittle sticks for a while,” she said at a recent forum. But she is not, in fact, whittling. She has launched a podcast, “Get MACED.”

Stephen K. Bannon, the former Trump adviser and podcast host, who reveled in their chaos, was one of the only people in Washington who said he would miss them.

“They were simply ‘too hot’ for the imperial Capitol,” Mr. Bannon said.

item.title: ‘Like the North Star’: Boston’s Citgo Sign Returns, 30 Feet Higher
item.description:
It has been called Boston’s “Big Ben,” inked onto the arms of die-hard Red Sox fans and used as a beacon by generations of disoriented Boston University freshmen finding their way back to campus.

So when the giant red, white and blue Citgo sign that towers over Kenmore Square went dark early this year, and then disappeared from the city’s skyline, its absence did not go unnoticed.

Its demise has often been predicted, in a city transformed by redevelopment. But on Thursday night, the 60-by-60 foot sign will be lit again, kicking off its latest incarnation in a new location 120 feet to the east and 30 feet higher.

“When you drive down Storrow and don’t see it, it’s weird,” said Ian Juras, 24, referring to Storrow Drive, the parkway beside the Charles River that carries traffic into Kenmore Square.

“We need it,” added his friend Meghan MacDonald, 26, looking up toward the soon-to-be- re-illuminated sign from Commonwealth Avenue on Tuesday night. “It’s like the north star.”

The sign will be easier to see on its new, taller perch, atop an addition to the same building on Beacon Street where it has sat for 60 years. Its new location makes the view of the sign less likely to be obstructed by future development, city officials said, ensuring it will continue beckoning runners to the homestretch of the Boston Marathon and baseball fans to Fenway Park.

Technically, the sign is a faithful replacement: After an inspection of its 11-foot-tall letters found severe deterioration, a Texas firm fabricated a shiny new C, I, T, G and O, which were trucked to Boston and raised to the rooftop in late summer. The glowing white square behind the blue letters has also been replaced, and the steel base beneath it rebuilt, an $8 million project paid for by Citgo.

All that remains is to flip a switch and watch the familiar red triangle blink back to life.

“Citgo may think of this as their sign, but in Boston, we think of it as ours,” said Sharon Durkan, a city councilor who represents the Kenmore Square neighborhood.

The first sign installed on the building was for Cities Service, the corporate precursor of Citgo, in 1940, when the company had a gas station on the ground floor. In 1965, when Cities Service rebranded itself as Citgo, the now-familiar logo was raised in its place. Six similar signs once stood in other cities; Boston’s is the sole survivor.

Assuring the sign’s long-term survival was a yearslong saga, marked by legal intricacies and moments when its removal seemed unavoidable. Preservationists saved it in 1983, after Citgo moved to take it down. In 2018, as concerns about neighborhood redevelopment mounted, then-Mayor Marty Walsh vetoed plans to make the sign an official landmark. Controversy erupted soon after, when a towering new sign nearby, for the tech company WHOOP, threatened to upstage the CITGO logo.

To undertake the sign’s rehab and relocation this year, project managers had to first secure federal “landmark sign” status. Because the sign was installed a few months before Lady Bird Johnson’s Highway Beautification Act was enacted, in 1965 — and would violate current federal standards with its size and visibility — any attempt to maintain or replace it without the protected status could have led to its permanent removal.

Every aspect of the sign’s existence seems steeped in complexity. It remains on the building via a long-term lease agreement between Citgo and the building’s owner, the real estate development firm Related Beal. But Boston University — the building’s former owner — still owns the land underneath it. Citgo itself, based in Texas, has been caught in corporate limbo; the court-ordered sale of its parent company, a subsidiary of Venezuela’s state-run oil company, has been on hold..

But to fans of the sign, its appeal is simple. Some have been slightly star-struck to discover that the letter C from the old sign is now enshrined near the pool table at Cornwall’s, Kenmore Square’s oldest continuously operated restaurant. Disbelief is not uncommon. “No one believes it’s the real C,” said Ms. MacDonald.

The sign’s absence for most of this year's baseball season was unnerving to Red Sox fans accustomed to its presence, a boxy talisman above the left field wall. (At least a few courted controversy, though, by asking aloud if the sign’s absence might have contributed to the team’s 15-game winning streak, which tied a franchise record in July.)

The sign has gone dark for much longer stretches. According to Citgo, the lights were turned off in 1979 at the request of then-Gov. Edward King to encourage energy conservation, and remained dark for the next four years. It transitioned from neon to LED in 2005, cutting its electric use in half, according to the company; in 2010, the technology was upgraded again.

Some have seen the Citgo sign as a symbol of Boston’s less gentrified past, and a way to hold onto that history, in an era when other Kenmore Square institutions — like the Rathskeller rock club, known as the Rat, which closed in 1997, and the historic Hotel Buckminster, which closed in 2020 — have become memories.

When the sign’s devotees rose up in 1983 to stop its removal, Robert Campbell, a longtime Boston Globe architecture critic who died last year, was among them. Mr. Campbell, who made the Big Ben comparison and called the sign a “crown jewel” of the city’s skyline, wrote an ode to it in the style of Oliver Wendell Holmes, who had protested the Navy’s plans to scrap the USS Constitution in 1830.

“Beneath it drummed the disco’s beat/ And burst the Red Sox roar,” Mr. Campbell wrote. “The meteor of Kenmore Square/ Shall sweep the clouds no more!”

In the neighborhood, where restaurants selling $60 steaks coexist with a McDonald’s walk-up window, life did not grind to a halt without the sign. At the Bluemoon Smoke Shop, employee Mac Makwana admitted he had mostly noticed its extended absence “when someone reminds me it’s not there.”

To Mark Handley, 40, a devotee of Kenmore Square who has watched, and embraced, its evolution, the sign matters most as a magnet pulling people to the neighborhood.

“Once you’re here,” he said, “you don’t need it.”

item.title: In Bending to Trump, Law Firm Did $11.8 Million of Free Work for Administration
item.description:
The future of Kirkland & Ellis was on the line.

President Trump, weeks into his second term, had begun an unprecedented campaign to target elite law firms with punitive executive orders that could hurt their profits.

A top partner at Kirkland, Mark Filip, scrambled to stave off the orders, signaling that he would be willing to negotiate with Mr. Trump’s personal lawyer and de facto enforcer, Boris Epshteyn.

Mr. Epshteyn, at a moment of maximum leverage, pressed Mr. Filip.

“You have a big trade practice, right?” Mr. Epshteyn wrote in a text message to Mr. Filip.

“Please call,” Mr. Filip replied.

The contours of the deal were outlined in a social media post by Mr. Trump in April 2025 in which he announced that Kirkland had agreed to do $125 million in pro bono work on causes Mr. Trump had championed, like helping veterans.

But a year and a half later, Kirkland has quietly disclosed to Congress that it has done an array of free work for the Trump administration, about 6,491 hours valued at $11.8 million, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times and interviews with five people familiar with the matter.

The records, including text messages and a seven-page letter the firm recently sent to Congress, offer the most detailed look yet at the terms of the deal. Kirkland has completed free work for the Commerce Department, the Pentagon, the Postal Service, the United States International Development Finance Corporation and an investment entity created as part of a trade deal between the United States and Japan, according to the five people and the letter.

The letter Kirkland sent to Congress came in response to requests from top Democrats — Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut; Senator Adam B. Schiff of California; and Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland — who have repeatedly pressed the firm to clarify the details of the deal. The three lawmakers are expected to have key oversight roles in Congress next year, when their party controls the House and Senate.

The disclosures demonstrate how Mr. Trump was not only able to make it more difficult for Kirkland to oppose him and his administration in court. He also successfully reshaped the firm into a tool of the state.

The revelations raise questions about whether the firm and the White House violated a longstanding federal law that makes it illegal for the federal government to accept free work, circumventing Congress.

In August 2025, The Times reported that Kirkland and Paul Weiss, the first firm to cut a deal with Mr. Trump, were doing work for the Commerce Department on trade deals. But until now, the breadth of the firm’s free legal work, including how many hours it worked for the government and the number of departments or agencies it worked for, had remained unclear.

Under the Antideficiency Act, the executive branch is limited in accepting free services, to ensure that an administration does not undertake efforts for which Congress has not appropriated money, or over which lawmakers cannot have oversight.

Zachary Price, a law professor at the University of California, San Francisco, and an expert in congressional appropriations, said that there were some exceptions to the act. But the arrangement between the law firms and the Trump administration, he added, “certainly violates the spirit of the law.”

“It amounts to expanded resources available for the executive without Congress providing them,” Mr. Price said.

In response to questions, Kirkland said in a statement that it had fully cooperated with the requests from lawmakers, and would “continue to cooperate.”

The firm said that its work did not violate the Antideficiency Act.

“First, the act does not apply where there is an agreement that the services will be provided for free, as there was here,” the firm said. “Second, the Antideficiency Act regulates the conduct of executive branch officials, not private parties like Kirkland.”

In the letter to lawmakers, the firm defended its independence, saying that it had declined to work on certain issues for the administration. Those include the U.S. Census, the pitched fight over the renaming of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, and the Postal Service plan to restrict mail-in ballots.

The firm also said that it had continued to represent transgender inmates on a pro bono basis, and had rejected a request from a veterans group supporting the construction of Mr. Trump’s triumphal arch.

In response to Kirkland’s disclosures, Mr. Blumenthal, Mr. Schiff and Mr. Raskin have urged other firms with ties to the administration to follow suit. Those include eight firms that made deals with the administration, as well as Sullivan & Cromwell, which represents Mr. Trump.

“The scope of Kirkland’s work for the administration indicates that we need to know from other firms how much, and what type, of work they did,” Mr. Blumenthal said in an interview. “The administration’s tactics smacked of implicit or overt threats, and we need to understand what led these other firms to capitulate.”

Shortly after he took office again last year, Mr. Trump issued a series of executive orders against law firms he believed had crossed him.

To the shock of the legal community, Paul Weiss capitulated to Mr. Trump, agreeing to do $40 million in pro bono work on causes Mr. Trump championed. In exchange, the president dropped a potentially crippling executive order against the firm that could have made it impossible to represent clients.

The firms were facing headwinds on a second front.

Kirkland was among 20 top law firms to receive a letter from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission demanding information about their “diversity, equity and inclusion (D.E.I.) related employment practices.”

Facing mounting pressure, Kirkland and a group of firms moved quickly to make deals. The intermediary, however, was not a government official, but a personal lawyer for Mr. Trump, Mr. Epshteyn.

In its letter to Congress, Kirkland acknowledged how the executive orders — and fighting them in court — could have jeopardized its relationships with clients.

“It would be rational for clients with matters before the federal government — be it transactions being reviewed for approval, investigations by agencies, or requests for product, device, or drug approvals — to not engage firms where they perceived the potential for adverse consequences solely on their choice of counsel,” the firm wrote.

The Paul Weiss deal, it added, functioned as a kind of blueprint.

It “set forth a precedent for how firms that wished to avoid immediately irreparable harm and protracted, intrusive litigation could resolve potential disputes with the administration,” the letter said.

To cut the deal, Kirkland said that it hired Ballard Partners, a lobbying firm with close ties to the White House, to arrange a meeting with Mr. Trump’s aides, including May Mailman, then a deputy to Stephen Miller, one of the president’s top advisers.

The firm also hired William A. Burck, the same lawyer who had struck the Paul Weiss deal with the White House, to negotiate with the employment commission.

Kirkland, in its letter, said that there was no underlying document that described the terms of the agreement — only Mr. Trump’s social media post announcing the deal. It noted that the administration had not asked it for an accounting of whether it had fulfilled its obligations.

item.title: A Paramedic Rushed to a Fatal Accident. The Dead Man Was Her Son.
item.description:
When Tricia Mumford, a paramedic in a rural county of Utah, was called to an emergency on Monday, it was clear the situation was dire. What she did not immediately know was that the victim was her own son.

That twist of fate only became clear while she was treating the man, whom the authorities said had been crushed by a neighbor’s car that he was trying to fix.

Logan Mumford, 28, of Sigurd, Utah, was beneath the car, trying to reach its alternator, when the scissor jack supporting it “suddenly gave way” and pinned him beneath the vehicle, the Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement on its Facebook page on Wednesday.

A neighbor who had been helping Mr. Mumford with the car was walking back to his house to retrieve lights and a hydraulic floor jack, a stronger tool, when he heard the car fall, the statement said. He ran back and tried to pull Mr. Mumford out or lift the car himself, but could not.

A 911 call was placed at 5:47 p.m., the sheriff’s office said, and deputies arrived as the neighbor returned with the floor jack and used it to free Mr. Mumford. He was unresponsive and had suffered “obvious significant trauma to the head,” according to the statement.

The first paramedic to arrive was his mother, according to the statement.

Ms. Mumford realized who she was trying to save only when she heard his name, the authorities said, and “did everything she could to save his life.” Mr. Mumford’s wife watched the rescue unfold, the statement added.

A medical helicopter landed nearby and airlifted him to Utah Valley Hospital in Provo, Utah. He was pronounced dead at the hospital.

Born in Logan, Utah, Mr. Mumford worked as a civil engineer, according to an obituary published by a local funeral home. He had attended Snow College and Utah State University and traveled as a missionary to Nicaragua.

The obituary described him as a “talented artist, a smooth dancer, a fitness enthusiast and a skilled mechanic.” He had a deep interest in cars, it said, once restoring a 1967 Ford Mustang in his parents’ garage “with little money and a lot of elbow grease.”

He married his wife in 2021, and the couple had two children, ages 3 and 1.

In its statement, the sheriff’s office reflected on the toll on its responders.

“We train for the unthinkable, and we answer the call when others need us most,” it said. “But no amount of training can prepare a mother to respond to an emergency involving her own child, or a wife to watch as the person she loves fights for his life.”

item.title: Los Angeles Prosecutor to Oversee Inquiry Into Mar-a-Lago Search
item.description:
The Justice Department has chosen Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, to oversee a key aspect of the so-called grand conspiracy case in Florida that has been scrutinizing Obama-era officials who have investigated President Trump, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Mr. Essayli will focus narrowly on the question of whether agents and prosecutors broke the law four years ago when they searched Mar-a-Lago, Mr. Trump’s private club and residence in Florida, the people said. The search was an early step in what ultimately led to an indictment of Mr. Trump by the special counsel Jack Smith on charges of mishandling classified documents and obstructing the government’s repeated efforts to retrieve them.

The decision to have Mr. Essayli work on an investigation into the Mar-a-Lago search was the latest shake-up in the grand conspiracy case, a crucial aspect of the president’s retribution campaign that has been plagued for months by a lack of focus and a wave of firings and resignations.

It also suggested that the central theory of the case — that the various investigations into Mr. Trump over the past 10 years or so were part of a single conspiracy to hurt his political prospects — may not be legally viable. Having tried for months to prove that Mr. Smith and other law enforcement officials were part of an overarching plot against Mr. Trump, prosecutors now appear to be pursuing smaller and separate lines of inquiry.

The move held personal significance for Mr. Essayli as well. Last month, a federal judge ruled that he has been illegally serving in his post in Los Angeles after remaining in the job beyond the 120-day limit set by law for acting U.S. attorneys. The Justice Department has said it will appeal that ruling, and a department official said Mr. Essayli will continue working in Los Angeles while also overseeing the investigation into the Mar-a-Lago search.

A spokesman for Mr. Essayli did not respond to messages seeking comment.

In recent weeks, the inquiry into the search has largely focused on efforts to get information from a group of former F.B.I. agents who took part in it. The former agents — many of whom were fired for having taken part in the classified documents case — received subpoenas this summer to appear before a grand jury in Federal District Court in Fort Pierce, Fla., on the theory that they might be able to offer evidence that the search was conducted illegally.

But lawyers for the former agents threw cold water on that theory in September. They asserted in court papers that if their clients were forced to testify in front of the grand jury, they would say that the search of Mar-a-Lago — like other aspects of the classified documents prosecution — was conducted fairly and in keeping with the law.

The lawyers raised another potential obstacle to their clients’ providing testimony: The judge who oversaw the classified documents case, Aileen M. Cannon, has barred Mr. Smith and members of his team from publicly discussing details of the investigation contained in a report about the case that was submitted after its conclusion. The lawyers have asked Judge Cannon whether the former agents can discuss the case in front of the grand jury without violating her order, but she has not yet issued a decision.

When the grand conspiracy investigation began late last year, the Justice Department seemed to be swinging for the fences in its efforts to appease Mr. Trump’s desire for revenge against a wide array of his most reviled opponents.

The inquiry initially sought to go after not only Mr. Smith but also other officials who tried to hold Mr. Trump accountable in other criminal inquiries. Chief among them were John O. Brennan, the former C.I.A. director, and James B. Comey, who ran the F.B.I. during Mr. Trump’s first term. Both men played important roles in the investigation into potential ties between Russia and Mr. Trump’s 2016 campaign.

But the broad investigation ran into a series of roadblocks — not least that there was little evidence that Mr. Smith, Mr. Brennan and Mr. Comey had actually conspired with one another. There were also seemingly insurmountable legal problems with seeking to connect events that occurred in different places — Washington and Florida, for example — over nearly a decade.

The first prosecutor who looked at the case, focusing on issues surrounding Mr. Brennan, was removed from the inquiry after she determined that there was no viable path toward bringing an indictment.

Other prosecutors stepped down in the months that ensued — including Joseph diGenova, a longtime Trump loyalist who was brought into the case this spring, promising to bring charges quickly. Two weeks ago, after the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections, Jason A. Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida who was nominally in charge of the investigation, also resigned amid growing dissatisfaction with his performance by his bosses in Washington.

Even before the midterms, the Justice Department had quietly signaled that it was no longer actively seeking to prove a grand conspiracy against Mr. Trump, but would instead carve out smaller prosecutions against his perceived enemies where it could.

Case in point: Prosecutors who had been working on the grand conspiracy case were instrumental in filing charges against Mr. Comey in Washington last month, accusing him of mishandling sensitive national security information that was published in an article in The New York Times.

item.title: Lawmakers’ Data Is Vulnerable to Trump’s Justice Department, Senator Warns
item.description:
A Democratic senator is urging Congress to secure lawmakers’ phone calls, emails and video meetings from the executive branch as President Trump threatens criminal investigations targeting members who conduct overly aggressive oversight of his administration.

The risk of retaliatory surveillance by the Justice Department, which could chill or blunt oversight as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress after the midterms, is a concern in part because many lawmakers use campaign-provided phones and personal email accounts for official business. Prosecutors have repeatedly subpoenaed communications companies for lawmakers’ records.

Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, said the Trump administration’s “threats to investigate members of Congress who do our job and oversee the executive branch are a five-alarm warning that the Senate needs to ramp up the security of our communications as soon as possible.”

The warning dovetails with concerns cited in a Senate report last week about “the threat of hacking and cyberattacks on senators and staff on their official and personal devices and accounts.” It directed the sergeant-at-arms office, the chamber’s technology provider, to study how “to provide end to end encrypted voice, video and text communications,” including storing data on its servers.

Lawmakers’ communications and data have repeatedly proved vulnerable.

One threat: foreign espionage. In 2024, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, then the majority leader, was among political leaders whose phones were targeted by Salt Typhoon, a Chinese hacking group that penetrated American telecommunications networks and surveilled the calls and texts of high-profile victims.

Criminal investigations pose another threat. During leak inquiries in the first Trump term, the Justice Department secretly obtained “non-content communications records for phone numbers and email addresses” of two Democratic lawmakers and dozens of aides from both parties, and “sought records of a Republican member of Congress,” according to an inspector general report.

In 2022 and 2023, prosecutors examining Mr. Trump’s attempt to subvert the 2020 election secretly subpoenaed phone logs of 20 current and former Republican lawmakers who had spoken with Mr. Trump or his proxies as they pushed allies to block certification of Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory around the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol. Those call logs, or “toll records,” show who communicated with whom and when, but not what was said.

As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and vow to investigate Mr. Trump and his inner circle, the administration has threatened criminal investigations in retaliation for oversight it deems unduly aggressive — raising the possibility that it could seize lawmakers’ communications and records.

Mr. Trump’s White House counsel, Will Scharf, warned that subpoenas deemed to lack a valid legislative purpose “may cross the line into blatant criminality” and “may warrant further investigation.” Aaron Reitz, a U.S. attorney in Texas, sent letters to Democratic lawmakers accusing them of planning to abuse oversight powers, citing civil rights crimes and demanding they preserve records and communications.

Any such attempted prosecution is unlikely to succeed because the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause gives Congress immunity for legislative acts. Still, the administration has repeatedly investigated Mr. Trump’s perceived adversaries on dubious legal and factual grounds, and exposed confidential law enforcement information to embarrass them.

In February, a grand jury rebuffed the Justice Department’s bid to indict several congressional Democrats for making a video reminding troops of their duty to disobey illegal orders. The White House released F.B.I. files last summer showing a former Democratic congressman whom Mr. Trump dislikes had confidentially admitted to agents a decade ago that he had sex with a woman who turned out to be a suspected Chinese spy.

The vulnerability of lawmakers’ communications records stems from ethics rules and gaps in federal law, said Christopher Soghoian, a technologist who recently left Mr. Wyden’s staff after a decade working on surveillance and cybersecurity.

Ethics rules prohibit lawmakers from using congressional resources to conduct campaign business like soliciting donations but allow official business using campaign resources. Most therefore use campaign-provided phones and consumer email accounts for all their communications — even as aides use work phones and government email addresses, he said.

“We have the 100 most important people in the Senate using cellphones and email accounts that are completely outside the perimeter, and the institution can’t protect them — it’s bananas,” Mr. Soghoian said. “Work-related communications of the entire institution are sitting on Yahoo or Google servers.”

Each chamber controls its own technology, and there appears to be little appetite for outside scrutiny of a widespread practice that invites awkward comparison to the scandal over Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server to conduct official business as secretary of state. The sergeant-at-arms office did not respond to inquiries, including how many senators, if any, use Senate-provided phones. Its House counterpart’s spokeswoman declined to comment.

In 2020, as Senate offices increasingly used cloud services like Google Documents and Slack on their own, the Senate inserted a provision into a bill adding some protections. The resulting statute allows Senate offices to ask courts to quash legal demands for their data and permits providers to disregard gag orders and notify Senate offices of such directives.

But major gaps remain. The law does not cover the House. It does not require companies to notify the Senate of such subpoenas, and senators cannot challenge directives they do not know about. Its text is ambiguous about coverage of campaign phones and private email accounts, and it created no system to alert companies when lawmakers are using those.

The Senate sergeant-at-arms office has sought to address some weaknesses by contractually requiring providers to notify the chamber of data demands. But a May 2025 letter from Mr. Wyden to colleagues warned that “significant gaps remain, especially for the campaign and personal phones used by most senators.”

Later in 2025, after revelations that prosecutors investigating Mr. Trump’s attempted subversion of the 2020 election had subpoenaed the phone logs of several Republican lawmakers, senators slipped a measure expanding the 2020 law into a bill ending a government shutdown. It required notification and clarified coverage of senators’ campaign and personal lines.

But it also allowed senators whose phone records were obtained without notice to sue and automatically collect $500,000 in taxpayer funds per record. It would have applied retroactively, creating a windfall for Mr. Trump’s Senate allies — though not his House ones. After a backlash, Congress repealed the entire measure, reopening the gaps.

At a February Senate oversight hearing on the election-case subpoenas, telecom lawyers testified that their companies had created a system to identify Senate-commissioned lines. They said they would notify Congress of subpoenas when possible and challenge nondisclosure orders in court.

They said they were working with the Senate sergeant-at-arms office to identify campaign and personal numbers used by lawmakers. But Mr. Soghoian described a haphazard system, with some Senate offices emailing telecom lobbyists their bosses’ numbers — meaning companies likely still do not know all the accounts that should set off notices if subpoenaed.

He also warned of broader threats. State and local prosecutors seeking political prominence could subpoena communications companies for congressional records. And while reports of spyware on legislators’ phones are common abroad, he said, they are rare in the United States because no one systematically looks for it.

Mr. Wyden has urged his colleagues to allow the sergeant-at-arms office to provide cybersecurity help for lawmakers’ campaign phones and personal online accounts, and to provide encrypted video and audio meeting software. That conversation has largely unfolded outside public view.

“I and other members have repeatedly urged Senate leaders — as recently as this summer — to secure our communications against surveillance by spies, criminals and the executive branch,” Mr. Wyden said.
